messages.subject: Multi-season occupancy without covariates
parts:
Hello there,

I am currently working on my master's thesis. For this, I have detection data from four years. I have transferred these into a table in binary form. The problem is that the covariates were only measured in one year (the last of the four years). Since these are vegetation data (e.g. shrub density), I do not want to apply them to all years, as some things may well have changed. Now I am faced with the problem of modelling a multiseason occupancy model without covariates. My question is: would the colext() or the occu() function be better? Theoretically, with occu() it doesn't matter how many years the data is from, since there are no covariates anyway, right? Or should I choose colext(), as it takes better account of occupancy in previous years? I can't get any precise information from the package info.

Another problem is that I was given data that came from nest box checking and trapping. Is it okay for the occupancy model to mix these two methods? Or does the model require independent methodology? Unfortunately, I have not found an answer in a search so far.

I am infinitely grateful for any help, as I have simply not found any clear info on these questions so far.


 Cheers,

Hendrik

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: AW: [unmarked] Multi-season occupancy without covariates
parts:
Dear Hendrik,

 

I really think that before we even ask a statistical question about which technique is better, we ought to ALWAYS state our biological questions. That is, the objectives of our statistical analysis. Without objectives, we can’t define what procedure is best. But since I always forget all this myself, I am not going to make a big deal of it now 😊

 

OK, so there is no problem at all using the dynamic model. It is actually better in two respects than using 4 static models (or one static model with a 4-level factor “Year”):

  • It gives you insight into the two processes that underlie changes in a species distribution: colonization and extinction
  • And by doing this, the model also corrects for temporal autocorrelation in the data

 

On the other hand, it is a more complex model, and all else equal, we ought to always use the simpler model. So, if you’re really not interested in the dynamics rates (col and ext), I might perhaps use occu() and not worry about temporal autocorrelation.

 

About the covariates: if you think they are mostly stable across the 4 years you might perhaps still add them as site covariates. If you find effects of them, then you can be almost sure than in reality these effects would be even more pronounced, since errors in x-variables lead to an attenuation of the slope estimates towards zero of covariates in a regression model.

 

Finally, different methods should not be a problem if the two kinds really sample the same statistical population of sites in a random way. Then, Method would just be a detection covariate with two levels. That’s one of the great things about these hierarchical models: you can neatly separate the process and the observation of the process.

 

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Multi-season occupancy without covariates
parts:
Dear Marc,

thank you very much for your answer.

The biological question is as follows. It is about gaining a better understanding of the presence and absence of the species. It was considered extinct in this area for a long time and was only rediscovered a few years ago and a monitoring programme has been running since then. An occupancy model can shed light on these issues and provide a more robust and accurate estimate of species abundance and distribution. This is part of my Master's thesis.

It is unfortunately not possible to distinguish between the nest box data and trapping data; I have previously considered this a weakness of the data base - what you say sounds very plausible though. The only covariate I would project with any degree of certainty to a period four and a half years ago would be tree density - this is likely to be fairly invariant. Likewise, the number of tree species in the transect should have remained stable. That would make two. Last year, however, not all sampling points were sampled at the same frequency - again, this is another variable that makes it considerably more difficult for me to create an adequate data basis at the moment.

My idea was: year 1 - 3 to create an occupancy model without covariates and for the fourth year to create a regression (e.g. binary logistic regression, as it currently lends itself due to the data sorting). However, your arguments have convinced me to look at the "constant" variables again.

The data come from >70 sampling sites. In fact, most of the time the traps are also set at a nest box site. Over the years, nest boxes remained unmoved and traps were (mostly) placed at the same sampling points (300 trapping nights per session).

I am currently leaning towards the occu() function and thus the "simpler" model.

I am delighted that I was able to get help so quickly.

Best regards

Hendrik

Thus, you may have some sites that are only surveyed during, say, years 1-2, while others will only have surveys during years 2-4 and so on. Such missing values in the data are virtually the rule in data sets used for occupancy models. Provided that these missing values occur at random, they can be ignored in the analysis. (Not occurring at random and not ignorable would for instance mean that you stop catching at sites where you don’t got anything earlier. That would mean that you have preferential sampling, see for instance the paper by Conn et al., MEE, 2017, and that needs to be modelled to avoid “wrong” inferences).

I am currently leaning towards the occu() function and thus the "simpler" model.

 

I am delighted that I was able to get help so quickly.

 

Best regards

 

Hendrik

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: AW: [unmarked] Multi-season occupancy without covariates
parts:
Dear Hendrik,

 

you don’t have to include method as a covariate. Moreover, you said that at many sites, for many occasions, both methods are employed simultaneously.

 

And yes, you may absolutely work with occu() with your kinds of covariates.

 

One additional thought though: when stacking the data year-wise and then using occu(), you might want to fit a random site effect to accommodate possible non-independence of occupancy at the same site over multiple years. For many of the model-fitting functions in unmarked, this can now be done, since Ken Kellner added the TMB software as an engine with which to fit models in unmarked. You can now use lme4- (or glmmTMB-)like notation to specify models with random effects. For instance, to fit an occupancy model with random site effects in occupancy (and constant detection), you would do this:

 

fm <- occu(~1 ~ (1|site), umf)

 

(I note that you must have data from multiple years to be able to fit a random site effect in occupancy. With data from just a single year, the associated variance parameter IS NOT ESTIMABLE.)

 

This random-effects option is really great. For instance, it would also allow to fit random observer effects in detection in the analysis of citizen-science data sets collected by many observers (provided observer ID is known).

 

Best regards  -- Marc

Hello there,

 

I am currently working on my master's thesis. For this, I have detection data from four years. I have transferred these into a table in binary form. The problem is that the covariates were only measured in one year (the last of the four years). Since these are vegetation data (e.g. shrub density), I do not want to apply them to all years, as some things may well have changed. Now I am faced with the problem of modelling a multiseason occupancy model without covariates. My question is: would the colext() or the occu() function be better? Theoretically, with occu() it doesn't matter how many years the data is from, since there are no covariates anyway, right? Or should I choose colext(), as it takes better account of occupancy in previous years? I can't get any precise information from the package info.

Another problem is that I was given data that came from nest box checking and trapping. Is it okay for the occupancy model to mix these two methods? Or does the model require independent methodology? Unfortunately, I have not found an answer in a search so far.

I am infinitely grateful for any help, as I have simply not found any clear info on these questions so far.


 Cheers,

Hendrik

Kery Marc schrieb am Donnerstag, 9. Februar 2023 um 14:09:11 UTC+1:

Dear Hendrik,

 

you don’t have to include method as a covariate. Moreover, you said that at many sites, for many occasions, both methods are employed simultaneously.

 

And yes, you may absolutely work with occu() with your kinds of covariates.

 

One additional thought though: when stacking the data year-wise and then using occu(), you might want to fit a random site effect to accommodate possible non-independence of occupancy at the same site over multiple years. For many of the model-fitting functions in unmarked, this can now be done, since Ken Kellner added the TMB software as an engine with which to fit models in unmarked. You can now use lme4- (or glmmTMB-)like notation to specify models with random effects. For instance, to fit an occupancy model with random site effects in occupancy (and constant detection), you would do this:

 

fm <- occu(~1 ~ (1|site), umf)

 

(I note that you must have data from multiple years to be able to fit a random site effect in occupancy. With data from just a single year, the associated variance parameter IS NOT ESTIMABLE.)

 

This random-effects option is really great. For instance, it would also allow to fit random observer effects in detection in the analysis of citizen-science data sets collected by many observers (provided observer ID is known).

 

Best regards  -- Marc

Hello Marc,

I have another question about this statement: "Then, Method would just be a detection covariate with two levels".

Is this simply an assumption that allows both methods in the end, or do I include the method as a covariate in the model? A find in a nest box is a "day quarter" as the species is nocturnal and a trap catch is "activity data" as the traps are overnight.

In conclusion, is it correct that with constant covariates (e.g. number of trees in the transect, number of tree species in the transect) I may continue to use the occu() function?

Hendrik schrieb am Mittwoch, 8. Februar 2023 um 15:27:38 UTC+1:

Dear Marc,

thank you very much for your answer.

The biological question is as follows. It is about gaining a better understanding of the presence and absence of the species. It was considered extinct in this area for a long time and was only rediscovered a few years ago and a monitoring programme has been running since then. An occupancy model can shed light on these issues and provide a more robust and accurate estimate of species abundance and distribution. This is part of my Master's thesis.

It is unfortunately not possible to distinguish between the nest box data and trapping data; I have previously considered this a weakness of the data base - what you say sounds very plausible though. The only covariate I would project with any degree of certainty to a period four and a half years ago would be tree density - this is likely to be fairly invariant. Likewise, the number of tree species in the transect should have remained stable. That would make two. Last year, however, not all sampling points were sampled at the same frequency - again, this is another variable that makes it considerably more difficult for me to create an adequate data basis at the moment.

My idea was: year 1 - 3 to create an occupancy model without covariates and for the fourth year to create a regression (e.g. binary logistic regression, as it currently lends itself due to the data sorting). However, your arguments have convinced me to look at the "constant" variables again.

The data come from >70 sampling sites. In fact, most of the time the traps are also set at a nest box site. Over the years, nest boxes remained unmoved and traps were (mostly) placed at the same sampling points (300 trapping nights per session).

 

I am currently leaning towards the occu() function and thus the "simpler" model.

 

I am delighted that I was able to get help so quickly.

 

Best regards

 

Hendrik

 

Kery Marc schrieb am Mittwoch, 8. Februar 2023 um 14:52:25 UTC+1:

Dear Hendrik,

 

I really think that before we even ask a statistical question about which technique is better, we ought to ALWAYS state our biological questions. That is, the objectives of our statistical analysis. Without objectives, we can’t define what procedure is best. But since I always forget all this myself, I am not going to make a big deal of it now 😊

 

OK, so there is no problem at all using the dynamic model. It is actually better in two respects than using 4 static models (or one static model with a 4-level factor “Year”):

  • It gives you insight into the two processes that underlie changes in a species distribution: colonization and extinction
  • And by doing this, the model also corrects for temporal autocorrelation in the data

 

On the other hand, it is a more complex model, and all else equal, we ought to always use the simpler model. So, if you’re really not interested in the dynamics rates (col and ext), I might perhaps use occu() and not worry about temporal autocorrelation.

 

About the covariates: if you think they are mostly stable across the 4 years you might perhaps still add them as site covariates. If you find effects of them, then you can be almost sure than in reality these effects would be even more pronounced, since errors in x-variables lead to an attenuation of the slope estimates towards zero of covariates in a regression model.

 

Finally, different methods should not be a problem if the two kinds really sample the same statistical population of sites in a random way. Then, Method would just be a detection covariate with two levels. That’s one of the great things about these hierarchical models: you can neatly separate the process and the observation of the process.

 

Best regards  -- Marc
